Theme

Body, health & movement

sex noun

intercourse

also have sex, sleep with, make love, intercourse, sexual intercourse

classical

Cic. N.D. 1.42; Liv. 4.2.6 (Lewis & Short)
Cels. 1.1
M-O s.v. sex

concubitus, concubitūs m.

noun, fourth declension

sexual intercourse

Properly a lying together; its usual sense is intercourse (Lewis & Short). To have sex with someone: cum aliquō concumbere (Cic. Fat. 30, Lewis & Short), or coīre.

Other words

  • rēs venereae — sex, the things of love

    noun phrase, plural · also used · classical · Cic. Sen. 47; Col. 9.14.3

    The plain, decent phrase of Cicero and Columella; venerius is the same word.

  • venus, veneris f. — love-making, sexual love

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Ter. Eun. 732: sine Cerere et Līberō friget Venus (Lewis & Short); M-O s.v. sex

    (chiefly in poetry and in Pliny and Columella)

    The goddess’s name used for what she presides over, as a euphemism.

  • coitus, coitūs m. — intercourse

    noun, fourth declension · also used · post-classical · Ov. M. 7.709; Suet. Cal. 25 (Lewis & Short)

    Not in Cicero in this sense (Lewis & Short); its general sense is a coming together.

  • stuprum, stuprī n. — illicit intercourse, debauchery, violation

    noun, second declension · avoid · classical · Cic. Tusc. 4.75 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 377: stuprum facere cum, have sex with

    Lewis & Short: dishonour by unchastity, debauchery, always as a disgrace; not a neutral word for sex, as Traupman gives it. Use concubitus or rēs venereae.

Examples

  • Concubitus vērō neque nimis concupīscendus, neque nimis pertimēscendus est.

    Sex should be neither too much desired nor too much feared.Cels. 1.1

See also fondle, love, play around with, screw, sex, sexual.
